title: What a choke is
summary: A choke is a narrowing of the barrel at the muzzle that keeps the shot together. It decides how wide the pattern is at the target, and the rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting say when you may change it.

body.html: When a shotgun fires, what leaves the muzzle is not a single bullet but a cloud of several hundred pellets. As it flies, it gradually spreads out. The mark this cloud leaves on a target or on a steel plate is called the pattern.

A choke is a slight narrowing of the barrel at the muzzle. It controls how quickly the shot spreads. A tighter choke keeps the shot together longer and gives a denser pattern for far targets. A more open choke lets it spread sooner and gives a wider, more forgiving pattern for close targets.

How much a choke narrows the barrel is called the constriction. For example, the inside of the barrel is 18.5 mm wide and the choke squeezes it to 18.0 mm, so the constriction is 0.5 mm. It is given in millimetres or in thousandths of an inch ('thou', also called 'points'). A barrel with no narrowing at all is called cylinder.

A wide pattern forgives small pointing errors on close targets. At long range, though, it thins out and leaves gaps that a target can slip through unbroken. A tight pattern stays dense further out but needs more precise pointing, so there is no single right choke, only one that suits the distance.

Most competition guns have interchangeable chokes: short tubes screwed into the muzzle with a choke key. Older guns may have fixed chokes machined into the barrel. Tubes from different makers often do not fit each other, and makers warn never to fire a multichoke gun without its tubes.

In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting targets fly at many different distances, so choosing chokes is part of your plan. In an over-and-under each barrel can have its own choke, for example a more open one for the first, closer shot and a tighter one for the second.

Coaches say things like 'quarter and half', 'open up the bottom barrel', 'go tighter in the top' or 'change chokes for this stand'. Names from cylinder to full, the fractions and the markings: Choke names, constrictions and markings.

The rules differ between disciplines. In Sporting™ chokes may be changed between stands, or between the singles and the doubles, if it causes no delay. Once the shooter has stepped onto the stand, they may not be changed. In Compak® Sporting the gun, barrels and chokes may not be changed within a round at all, only between rounds, except after a breakdown.

notes.html: Keep choke names exactly as the coach says them. Do not convert them into millimetres: the values differ between makers.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: What chokes are you using? — Quarter and half.
phrases.meaning: Improved cylinder in one barrel, modified in the other.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Put quarter in the bottom and half in the top — the second bird is longer.
phrases.meaning: More open choke for the first, closer target; tighter for the second, farther one.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Open up — these are all close.
phrases.meaning: Fit more open chokes because the targets are near.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Check your tubes are tight before the round.
phrases.meaning: Make sure the choke tubes have not loosened.

key_points.html: The pattern is the mark the shot cloud leaves on a target or plate.
A choke narrows the muzzle: tighter for far targets, more open for close ones.
Interchangeable tubes are screwed in with a choke key; makers warn never to fire without them.
Choose the choke for the distance at which you will shoot.
Sporting™: change chokes between stands, not on the stand; Compak® Sporting: no change within a round.

did_you_know.html: Choke constrictions are tiny. Even a full choke narrows a 12-gauge bore by only about 1 mm in diameter. That is about 0.5 mm on each side, less than the thickness of a bank card.

quiz.q: Which choke gives the widest pattern?
quiz.explain: Cylinder has no constriction, so the shot spreads soonest.

quiz.q: What happens if you increase the constriction?

options.text: The pattern stays tighter for longer
The shot leaves the barrel faster

quiz.explain: More constriction keeps the shot together longer, so at the same distance the pattern is narrower and denser.

quiz.q: Why is a very open choke a poor choice for a far target?

options.text: It gives far more recoil than others
It is banned for targets over 30 m
At range the pattern thins out, with gaps
It wears the barrel out much faster

quiz.explain: A wide pattern thins out at long range, and the target can slip between the pellets.
